speechtext: CONGRATULATIONS ON ATTAINMENT OF HIS 73ld BIRTHDAY-HON. C. G. POWER: 30th ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION TO PARLIAMENT

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, according to the morning press, today is the anniversary of two very interesting events in Canadian history : one was the birthday in Canada seventy-three years ago of a child who later became Prime Minister of this country and is Prime Minister at the present time. Another was the entry into the House of Commons thirty years ago of a young man who has been here ever since and is with us still. I refer to the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power).
On behalf of my associates and myself I wish to congratulate them both. This is one occasion when we can forget party differences and pay deserving tribute to two men who have given a large proportion of their lives to the service of their country.
I want to compliment the Prime Minister upon having reached another milestone in his career. Seventy-three years is three years over the allotted span given to man. I wish to compliment the Prime Minister upon looking so hale and- hearty in spite of his years, and we wish for him many more years to enjoy life as one of Canada's elder statesmen.
I want to compliment the hon. member for Quebec South as well. His has been a familiar figure here for more than three decades. I understand it is the longest continuous record without defeat of any living member of the House of Commons. During that period it was his privilege to have a most honoured record in two world wars. Whatever the future holds for the hon. member we shall always have pleasant memories of our association with him in this house. Whatever his future course may be 1 am sure he will take with him the best wishes of a host of friends not only inside this parliament but outside as well.
Right Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Veterans Affairs): Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my colleagues on this side of the house, and I think on behalf of every single member of the house, I desire to express my
deepest gratitude to the hon. the leader of the opposition for his typically generous and well-deserved words.
Only a few months ago I had the honour, on another very significant occasion, of paying my personal tribute to my distinguished Prime Minister, and, on this great anniversary when he is seventy-three, we who are with him, around him and behind him to the limit-and I am speaking without the slightest political tinge-only hope that at eighty-three he will be in the same seat and still leader.
My friend said a very true thing. There are occasions on which we forget the acerbities and the asperities of political animosities and when we are able to rally together as Canadians honouring one who has honoured himself in the great service he has rendered to Canada. And so, sir, on behalf of this side of the house may I be privileged this afternoon to extend to you the hope for many, many continued years of great happiness, of great content and of great continued service to the country you love so well.
May I say a word to the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), one who is my best friend in the house. We were two of the greatest fellow sinners in the historic years between 1930 and 1935. I hope that for our sins during those historic years we shall be forgiven. But this at least I may say, sir. Although we exposed some terrible policies we established some faithful and enduring friendships. May I say humbly that the cause of democracy, the cause of freedom, the cause of those who have been wrongly called the common people, and whom I prefer to call the ordinary people, the simple, plain people of our country, have never had a finer champion in this Canadian confederation than the Hon. Charles Gavan Power, the member for Quebec South. May I at the same time, as his fellow sinner, extend to him very warmhearted felicitations.
Chubby.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes, Chubby, beloved by everyone in this house. May I extend to him the greetings of every single member of every part in this house, and express what I believe to be the common wish, that he may long continue to devote that splendid and brilliant brain of his to the service of

his province, of the nation and of all the freedom-loving nations of the world.

Mr. Speaker, after what has been said both by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Bracken) and by the right hon. the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) there is not much left for me to say on behalf of the party with which I am associated in this house.
I should like, first, to convey to the Prime Minister our very best wishes and our sincere greetings and to say to him that we trust he will be spared many years to enjoy the honours that have been bestowed upon him.
To the hon. member for Quebec South I vould say that we are delighted to have the opportunity today of congratulating him also.
[ have always felt that in the hon. member for Quebec South we had a colleague with broad, humanitarian sympathies, which sympathies he showed in the high office he held during the war, while he looked after the interests of many of our young men who served in the armed forces.
While my remarks may be brief, I assure the Prime Minister and the member for Quebec South that they are none the less sincere.
Mr. SOLON E. LOW (Peace River): It is always a good thing, it seems to me, that we have birthdays and anniversaries. In this instance it gives us a chance in this house to let the Prime Minister and the hon. member for Quebec South know that if in the smoke of battle we treat them with some severity, we are happy to have this opportunity of showing them uncommon kindness lest they think we are their enemies.
We have no enmity personally towards anyone, and we wish to let the world know that is true. I take this opportunity therefore, on behalf of the Social Credit group in this house, of expressing our sincere congratulations to the Prime Minister on reaching the age of seventy-three and at the same time of keeping his vitality so high. I believe I said on the occasion of his seventy-second birthday that it was a secret which I thought a good many, people in the country would like to find out, how he could reach such an age and still keep his vitality at that level. It is also a secret, the answer to which a good many people would like to discover, how it is that although the Prime Minister has attained such a ripe age the people continue to put him and his government back in power. For the last twenty years, as far back as I 
can remember anything political in my life, the people of the country were going to "throw Mackenzie King out".
Seriously, Mr. Speaker, I do wish for the Prime Minister the attainment of every single thing his heart desires except one, and I believe he can easily guess what that is. At the same time I wish to take this opportunity to extend to him our sincere wishes for a very happy Christmas season.
To our good friend the member for Quebec South, let me express our congratulations on his achievement as well. Thirty years of continuous public service is no mean achievement, Mr. Speaker, especially during the trying times that Canada has been witnessing in . recent years. We have the highest admiration for the splendid work the hon. member did during the last war. We feel that he achieved a standard of administration in the public service that will for many years be a challenge to anyone in this country who thinks of entering public life.
To both gentlemen we extend our heartiest congratulations.

Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs):	Mr. Speaker, it is quite obvious from what is going on in the house that this day marks a festive occasion for the province of Quebec. It would not be necessary, for all to be convinced of that fact, that anyone should add a few words in French in order to associate an overwhelming majority of the people of my prov-* ince who speak my own language to the tribute which is being paid to the leader of our party and to my excellent friend and fellow-member for a constituency of the city of Quebec. But I think that the record of this tribute would remain incomplete if it did not include a few w'ords in French.
Nearly thirty years ago, we placed our confidence in the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King on the occasion of the 1919 convention. We have had no reason to regret it ever since. From year to year we have become more and more convinced that he had no more real or keener wish than to associate all Canadians, whatever their origin, their language or their creed, in the privileges and responsibilities of Canadian citizenship. I believe that he has thus rendered an inestimable service not only to the people of my province, my creed and my race, but to Canada at large.
Of course, "Chubby" and I have been lifelong friends and one has reason to be proud of the tribute paid to him by all his colleagues in this house. No one has helped

Anniversaries-Mr. King and Mr. Power
more in the life work of our Right Hon. Prime Minister than the man who has for thirty years represented Quebec South in this house. It is a rare but most fortunate coincidence that we should be able, on a single occasion, to include in similar tributes, the Right Hon. the Prime Minister, William Lyon Mackenzie King, and the Hon. Charles Gavan Power.
I want to say in French that there is no one I know, speaking my own language, who is not desirous to associate himself in the wishes and tributes we are tendering to both these gentlemen.
(Text):

Mr. Speaker, as one of the younger members of this honourable assembly, perhaps for the first time in twenty-five years I may be privileged to pay tribute to one who has been serving Canada, the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), my courteous, kind and considerate friend for a quarter of a century. And may I be permitted to couple with his name, sir, that of my dear friend the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power).
The British Order of Merit has been bestowed upon our Prime Minister; all honour to him in accepting it. We in this chamber will not forget that it is emblematic. Today we have the honour and privilege of paying respect to these two gentlemen, as emblematic of a united Canada and of everything worthwhile not only to our own country but to civilization itself.
The tact, judgment, kindness, and consideration of these two honourable gentlemen have been appreciated by all of us, whether they were on this side of the house or on that. I suppose it would be quite natural for me to say that we were happier when they were on this side. But wherever they are, we honour and respect them. We hope and pray to God that they may be privileged to serve this country for many years to come-on this side; and we in turn will do our level best to serve Canada on the side on which we belong.
Now that the Prime Minister and my dear friend the hon. member for Quebec South have reached the age when flowers are being presented, I do not think they would mind retiring to a position of ease and contentment. But even if they do, I say to the people of Canada that they will be well served by my right hon. friend and the hon:. member for Quebec South, representing as they do not only two elements in the country but a united Canada, a people with the same objectives in their hearts as to the welfare
of our native land and the welfare of civilization, in order that we in Canada may serve better the rest of our fellowmen in these most difficult times. I offer congratulations to the Prime Minister and to the hon. member for Quebec South.

Mr. Speaker, I met Mr. King for the first time nearly a quarter of a century ago because I had defeated his own candidate by 3,500 votes. I must say that one of my constituents impersonated the hon. member for Quebec South, and told the die-hard Liberals that he was a personal messenger sent by Mr. King to advise them to vote against the government candidate. Mr. King had invited me to luncheon at Laurier House with Mr. Lapointe. It was the most successful of all peace conferences.
I shall never forget that occasion. It afforded me the privilege of becoming acquainted with the real Mr. King, whom Canadian and foreign historians and writers have so often and so wrongly described as somebody so like the Grand Lama of Tibet that even the Liberal caucus wondered at times if he was a mar-morean statue or a human being. They did not realize that he is the busiest man in Ottawa and that, owing to his high sense of public duty, he feels obliged to sacrifice his social life to his responsibilities as Prime Minister and leader of the Liberal party.
I wanted my electors to know Mr. King as well as I knew him. The first time he stopped at Riviere du Loup he was at the back of his car and was met by a handful of my friends. Years later, when he was leader of the opposition, I invited a few people to my house to shake hands with him. They came by hundreds. The third time 25,000 people had gathered at Riviere du Loup from all around on the occasion of the visit of the king and queen. Mr. King was there. Mr. King is so popular and so well liked because his natural gifts of kindness and cordiality always bloom out in a climate of mutual confidence and affection.
On another occasion, we were then in the cold region of opposition, and in Riviere du Loup it was at least fifteen below zero. Mr. King had been driving eighty miles at night from Edmundston to Riviere du Loup. We did our best to warm him up at home.
Another time the circumstances were not the same. It was the funeral of Mr. Lapointe in my church at Riviere du Loup. Mr. King was coming down the aisle with Mr. Cardin; we shook hands, and we did not say a word.
It has been repeated time and time again that Mr. King was subtle in a Machiavellian way, and that he could cut the throat of an

Anniversaries-Mr. King and Mr. Power
opponent by a very delicate gesture of his hand. But my own experience was altogether different. The ties of friendship between Mr. King and myself were strong enough to resist disagreement, contradiction and opposition; even displeasure did not break them. After having been an active supporter of his for twenty years, to my profound regret I crossed the floor of the house on the conscription issue.
At the following general election he was coming from the maritimes. I knew he was to pass through Riviere du Loup, and although I was temporarily on the other side of the tracks, I found the door of his car wide open for me. Without asking me anything, he gave good advice to the crowd that was there. He said, "Vote for my friend Jean Frangois Pouliot," and he was cheered to the echo.
Remembering my close association of so many years with Mr. King, and remembering also that my electors of Riviere du Loup have known him better than the bureaucrats of the pen who have depicted him as so aloof and so inaccessible, I must admit that I am very human and that he is also very much so; but I hasten to say that I would willingly trade fifty per cent of my humanity for fifty per cent of his industry. We all wish for the Prime Minister that his industry will continue to serve humanity. I wish him a happy birthday and a happy Christmas; and I wish the hon. member for Quebec South a pleasant anniversary and a merry Christmas.

Mr. Speaker, while this gives an ordinary membeir of the house an opportunity to wish everyone a merry Christmas and happy New Year, at the same time it gives us the opportunity to pay tribute to someone; and today I do that sincerely because I am paying a tribute to one who is a native son of my own county, of which I am also a native son. I dio not need to pay any tribute to the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), because we have known each other for many years, and indeed on some occasions I think we have been stuck with each other. So I need pay him no particular tribute because in every sense of the word we are pals. .
I rise on this occasion, Mr. Speaker, because I feel that as a representative from Waterloo county' I would be remiss in my duty if I did not pay my compliments to a native son. Ours is a peculiar county; it might be called a melting pot, because it is made up of people from almost all the countries of the world. Out of that melting pot has come a virile Canadian citizenship, a people loving Canada, loving the empire and all the freedoms for which it stands. So today w'hea I address

these remarks to the Prime Minister I do so realizing that during all the years we have fought each other politically we have always had a great love for our native county. When the right, hon. gentleman returned to Waterloo county just a few months ago the acclaim he received was not offered because he happened to be the leader of the Liberal party; it was because a native son of our county had achieved a great success. So, Mr. Prime Minister, let me say in all sincerity that I pay tribute to you today as a native son of Waterloo county who has achieved great success. We may differ in our policies; we may differ in certain principles we hold; we may differ politically; nevertheless it is a tribute to our county that one of its sons should have been chosen to lead the government of Canada for so many years. Today I stand here as one who is politically opposed to you, but as a member of this House of Commons who believes in the freedom we have enjoyed and tried to preserve in this country. I pay tribute to you, sir, for having done your duty as you saw it and for having ted this country through a most- difficult period. If it is possible to do so later I should like to shake your hand, and say, "Well done, Waterloo!"

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Some years ago, Mr. Speaker, I was much impressed by a passage I read-I think it was by George Eliot-in which appeared the words:
Speech is but broken light upon the depth of the unspoken.
I was much impressed with the significance of those words at that time. But they have come to have a new and fuller meaning this afternoon, one for which I cannot be too grateful. and for which I cannot thank the members of this house too warmly. All that has been said by the leaders of the different groups opposite, by my colleagues on either side of me, by other fellow members from this and the opposite side of the house, has touched me more deeply than I can begin to express. I hope they will understand that, while I am deeply in their debt for the kindness of heart they have revealed, it is only because I feel as deeply as I do that I am unable in return to express to the house the debt I feel I owe to its members for these many evidences of their friendship and great good will. To one and all I am profoundly grateful for the congratulations and good wishes which have been so generously extended on my seventy-third birthday anniversary.
The wish has been very kindly expressed that I might continue in public life for a considerable, time longer. No one knows what the

Anniversaries-Mr. King and Mr. Power
future holds in store. As, however, I look at the beautiful basket of flowers immediately in front of me, and see that in number the roses represent seventy-three years, I realize only too well that, with the years, the number is rapidly becoming far too large.
I should like to take advantage of this moment, if hon. gentlemen opposite will allow me, to express my appreciation, particularly to hon. members on this side of the house who have presented me with this gift, together with the good wishes they have *expressed, accompanied by a scroll containing their names individually and including the entire membership of our party in the house. This parchment is something which I shall treasure deeply all my life, and which I hope, when I am gone, may find its place in the public archives of our country.
This is the seventy-third anniversary of my birthday. In many ways I could wish the figures might be reversed, and that it might be the thirty-seventh anniversary. Looking back over the shears, I would say that had I been able to glimpse at thirty-seven what I have lived to see since, or had I been able to surmise it, I wonder very much if I should have felt at that or any time that I could ever accept office and assume the responsibilities that have come with office in the years that have followed since.
Reference has been made to the county of Waterloo. I think it was just four years before that thirty-seventh anniversary that I had the honour of being elected the member for 'North Waterloo. It was a year later that I had the honour of being made a member of Sir Wilfrid Laurier's government as the first Minister of Labour. Little did I suspect, at that time, that a political career awaited me through the years, or that any career would begin to present the problems and responsibilities that have come with the years. I wonder if any of us, if we could see ahead for the next twenty or thirty years, would be able to pursue our tasks with equanimity of mind. Yet, speaking honestly, as the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdon-nell) has questioned me for saying, looking back over the years I think I can say that, great as the anxieties and trials have been, at times, what there has been of so-called burdens of office over those strenuous years have been far outweighed by the rewards of public service. Of those many rewards, I can think of none greater than the one which has come to me this afternoon in this House of Commons. I am indeed grateful to all hon. members for that. How much all that has come to me of opportunity and reward is
owing to the sacrifices, privations and sufferings of others no one realizes more fully than myself.
May I say this further word. It relates more particularly to the future. I believe all hon. members of this house and of the parliaments which will succeed this one will have great responsibilities to bear. We have seen difficult times in the past; but I would not speak my heart honestly this afternoon if I did not say I believe we were going to witness very serious times in the years to come. I think every member of any free parliament must consecrate his life as never before to the furtherance of good will, to the utmost of his ability; and to a determination to battle evil forces as he never has battled them before.
I hope every individual member will, to the utmost of his power, wherever opportunity comes, do what he can both as between individuals and between nations to foster the utmost of good will; but, at the same time, be prepared as an individual, as we must be prepared as a nation, to use every instrument in our power to battle the forces of evil whenever and wherever they raise their heads.
I am sure we must all bend our energies in that direction; and, if we do, I have not the slightest doubt that, having played the part that the different nations of the British commonwealth with their allies have played in preserving liberty and freedom in this world, come what may, liberty and freedom will be preserved through future generations and in the same courageous way, if that is necessary.
In facing the unknown, there is only one sure path to follow. It is, from day to day, to the best of one's judgment and ability, to perform the duty which is closest at hand, sustained by the belief that, "As thy days, so shall thy strength be."
Little has given me more pleasure this afternoon than that there should have been associated with my name on this anniversary the name of another who has been a very close colleague through many years, and who is so greatly honoured and beloved by members of this House of Commons. I refer, of course, to the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power). It is true that, in point of number of years of membership in the house, I still am a little in advance of him, a little over a year; his time may come but meanwhile I will not allow anyone else to assume the role of dean of this house, who cannot meet its requirements to the full.
Let me say, however, that thirty years of continuous and unbroken service as a member

Anniversaries-Mr. King and Mr. Power
of this House of Commons is a record of which the oldest no less than the youngest member might be enviable. It is one all of us are proud the member for Quebec South has made. I extend to him both personally and on behalf of the party I represent-indeed, as hon. members appear to wish to have it, on behalf of the house-the heartiest congratulations and the warmest and best wishes for his future.
I should like with the permission of hon. members, to mention at this time one or two other hon. members who have been in the House of Commons for a long time, and whose association with its business through the years I have been here, it has been the privilege of my hon. friend from Quebec South and myself, to share. The hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) has been kind enough to extend greetings in terms which touched me deeply. May I say he has been an associate of Mr. Power and myself for over twenty-six continuous years, and I extend to him the warmest congratulations and best wishes, on the record he also has made. I reciprocate toward him in fullest measure all the kindly feelings he has expressed towards myself.
There is one other hon. member who shares with the hon. member for Danforth the record of over twenty-six years of continuous service in the House of Commons. I refer to the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) who, unfortunately, is not with us today. Through illness he has been prevented from taking his seat at this session. A day or two ago, when I learned of the serious nature of his illness, I took it upon myself to send him a telegram -not personally only, but on behalf of all members of the House of Commons-to express to him the solicitude we felt concerning his health, and how earnestly we hoped he might soon be restored to health and able to take his seat in the house again.
There are other hon. members who have been here for quite a long time. Somewhat hurriedly I have prepared a list of those who have been in the house for over twenty-one years. Among those who have been in the house for over twenty-one years are the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas (Mr. Cas-selman), the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie (Mr. Raymond), the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe), the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black), the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette), the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Ilsley)' and the hon. member for York East

(Mr. McGregor). There may be others, but I believe I have covered all of those who have been here for more than twenty-one years.
Then there are some, like my colleague the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie), who have been associated with politics in legislatures as well as in parliament, and whose combined years of public service would extend over a very long period.
May I say to these old-timers, these old friends, how deeply I have appreciated the association we have had together through the years, and how warmly I wish for them all that is best in the future.
May I, in conclusion, thank all hon. members of the House of Commons for what their association has meant to me in the years I have been in this house-and it has never meant more than it has today. I hope each one will believe that from my heart I extend to him and to her, the very best of wishes for the future, all that one could wish for what is best in their lives.
With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I should like to add a word of thanks and also of good wishes to hon. members of the other house with whom through the years I have shared public life in this parliament; and also my thanks to members of the fourth estate, my friends and fellow members of the parliamentary press gallery whose friendship has also helped greatly to enrich my life, and for whose futures, I extend my best wishes.

Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a happy occasion, and perhaps for me a happy coincidence, that the birth of the Prime Minister of Canada and leader of the House of Commons should coincide with the thirtieth anniversary of my entry to this chamber. It has permitted hon. members who were kind, generous and courteous enough to pay the usual compliments to persons in my position, to couple my name with that of the Prime Minister.
They have been most kind. They have shown that in this House of Commons, even in the midst of an emergency session, one may take time out to deal with matters which ordinarily might be considered as indications of frivolity and perhaps a lack of interest in affairs of state, but which really might better be considered as indications of the spirit of good will in the House of Commons, the spirit of friendship, the spirit of comradeship and of chivalry which is characteristic of this Canadian nation of ours, and which is so well represented by the members of the house.
My right hon. friend the Prime Minister has made some reference to the competition which might exist between us for fatherhood of this house. Speaking for myself, when I

Anniversaries-Mr. King and Mr. Power
look at the brood of children which throngs the benches of this chamber I would say to the Prime Minister that I wish him well in his role of father to all those who sit about him. I also admit freely he has, through his kindness, his fatherly affection and guidance, all the qualities and qualifications of a father in a degree far superior to mine.
For many years the paths of the Prime Minister and myself have followed along parallel lines, although at all times they may have been on vastly different planes. Both of us have taken active parts in political life. For my part I have enjoyed the relationship which has existed between us. of an admiring and devoted1 follower to a respected chieftain. If at times our paths have diverged, there was in no respect a lowering of the honour in which I held him or a lessening of the gratitude which I have had for his kindness. So strong has that attachment been, and it still persists, that I rarely neglect him in my prayers. As one of the few of us who are still continuing Liberals, I pray that he will return to the faith of his forefathers.
You have probably often speculated, Mr. Speaker, as I have, when at the beginning of a session you hear addresses made with respect to those who are no longer here, as to just what will be said about you. If you want to resolve that speculation all you have to do is remain twenty-five years more in this house. You will then be a witness to a full-dress rehearsal. You will also have an advantage over those others in that if hon. members who are making the addresses or observations with respect to you forget to mention salient points which you believe to be important in connection with your career-after all, you know better than those who are speaking about you-you can rise on a question of privilege the next day and correct them.
I have spent half' of my life as a member of this house. It has been a good half life. It has been joyous; it has been one filled with comradeship and kindness. There are no moments of it which I regret. I say that with perfect sincerity. There are those who have the idea that politics is a mean kind of game, that it is filled with disappointments and delusions, but so far as I am aware, and *co far as I have been able to observe during ail these years, politics is filled also with loyalties, with decencies, with honesties, with comradeship, with evidence of the helping hand and the sympathetic spirit. I for one can say that it has been a wonderful life and a good one, and I do not regret it.
My right hon. friend the Prime Minister has often expressed the wish to write a book. That desire comes to almost all of us who have taken some part in public life. I too have thought that perhaps in my retirement I might solace my years and days with the writing of a book. It would not be concerned with the mazes of statecraft nor with the intricacies of international affairs. I should like to write a book about this Commons House of Canada. I perhaps would put it in the form of a homily, ashes to ashes and dust to dust, and I would entitle it "Back to Front and Back Again". I would tell of the long and painful progress down five rows of seats to the front benches, and I would tell also of the short and rapid and sudden transition from a private car to an upper berth. I would perhaps dedicate it to the over-ambitious youth who inhabit the back benches and also to the over-pretentious elderly ones who inhabit I he front benches. I might comment on the title page in ancient Greek, "Mati-otes, Matiotetoun Ta Panta, Matiotes"- "Vanity of vanities; all is vanity".
I cannot close these remarks without making some reference to the constituency of Quebec South which during all these years has shown such patience, tolerance and indulgence in sending me here to represent them, alien though I was in birth and language. That constituency has shown me a measure of confidence which is rare indeed in parliamentary history, and for which I shall be forever grateful.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, may I for a moment forgo parliamentary rules, in the strict sense of the term, to direct a few words to my friends and colleagues of the province of Quebec.
My friends, for years we have stood together in struggle and in triumph, we have been friends in good times and bad. In Canada, I stand as a living example of the tolerance and broad-mindedness characteristic of our fair province since, for thirty years, electors whose language and racial background are other than my own, have been so kind as to return me as their representative.
Hear, hearl

May I thank my colleagues for their unfailing support and friendship. May I also ask you gentlemen to convey my thanks to those leaders and constituents of yours with whom, in the past, I often rejoiced over your victories.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MESSAGE OP THANKS FOR WEDDING PRESENT PROM CANADA
speechtext:
Before I ask a page to carry this basket of flowers to my private office, I should like to inform the house that I received last night, in a communication from our High Commissioner at London, a letter which I should like to read, from Her Royal Highness Princess Elizabeth, thanking the government and the people of Canada for the wedding gift which was presented to her: Buckingham Palace
5tli December, 1947.
Dear Mr. Mackenzie King:
I am most grateful to the government and people of Canada for the wedding present of such remarkable generosity which they have sent me. They have given me a collection of silver so magnificent, both in quality and in quantity, that my pride in its possession is only equalled by my pleasure that the people of Canada should have seen fit to express their good will towards ine in this way.
Not content with this splendid present they have sent me in addition a mink coat of absolute perfection. Whenever I wear it, as I very often shall, it will remind me of the moving tributes and marks of affection which have reached me from all over Canada during these last few weeks and which have left a very deep impression on me. Should anyone wish to know what an austerity program is, if he would visit the United Kingdom at this time he would get a very good idea of what such a program can be. It means no private motoring, it means meagre and monotonous food rations, a minimum of clothing, a minimum of those purchases which add to the amenities of life.
Ours is a restrictive program for a temporary period of time. We are cutting off many imports, such as strawberries in February, to which we have become accustomed but with which we can very well do without. Certain items that assist in the amenities of housekeeping are either cut off or are made more expensive or in some cases are limited in quantity to Canadian production. Certain restrictions will be placed on the import of capital goods which will have the effect of cutting down types of construction that can just as well be postponed. But I hope that no one will believe that the government considers this a real austerity program. Having seen an austerity program in operation, I hope that such a program will not be necessary in Canada.
At the last sitting of the house we heard from the official opposition two solutions of the Canadian problem. One of them we can accept wholeheartedly while the other we must reject as wholly undesirable and incapable of making any contribution to our objective.
The member for Calgary West advocated increased production. That is the government program. He spoke of increased developments in his own province, particularly in the fields of oil and coal. I may tell hon. members that the government has that type of expansion very much in mind. The possibilities for increased oil production have been explored and I can tell hon. members that the objective for the Leduc field, which is Canada's new producer, is 250 producing wells by the end of 1948. Production on such a scale will be an important contribution to the correction of Canada's United States exchange balance.

I will not refer to the theory of money as it relates to devaluing the currency. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has dealt with that subject. I wish to refer to the by-products of that policy. As we all know, the devaluation of currency is a device which makes it possible for the owner of a business to sell his products in foreign markets for one kind of money and to pay his help and his costs of production with a less valuable kind of money. The theory is that such an arrangement will enable his firm to export to markets which otherwise would not be available. That objective is not important at the present time. There is no market in the world which Canada's prices will not permit Canada's goods to enter. However, that is usually the purpose of devaluing currency.
As far as the Canadian worker is concerned, he is paid in money less valuable than that received by his employer. Of course the effect of that is to write down his wages. And incidentally, at the same time as his wages are written down, his savings are written down because his savings are transferred from a money of one value into a less valuable money. In time the situation will be corrected, in that the worker will not be satisfied to accept the same number of dollars of less value. He will insist on getting a greater number of those dollars and by that means he may be put back in balance. Even so,

speechtext:
For reasons which I shall develop, the schedule is not exhaustive; that is, it does not cover all the capital goods and related products the imports of which it may be desirable to regulate. It is not intended to restrict imports for normal repair, maintenance and servicing, with the exception of repair parts for automobiles, which will be dealt with by special quota arrangements. Since the only practical way for the customs department to administer the restrictions is to have a complete ban on specified tariff classifications of imports, subject only to exception by permit, repair parts have been excluded, except in the case of automobile repair parts as I mentioned, from the tariff items listed in schedule III.
The category of imports for which permits will be required is basically that going into new and expanded construction and equipment. These will have to be determined on a "project" basis. That is, the application for any specific import will require detailed information on the purpose. If the project as a whole is approved1 a project number will be assigned which will ensure that not only the particular import applied for, but all imports listed under schedule III necessary to the completion of the project will be permitted.
The project approach will not only simplify the administration, but avoid possible confusion or uncertainty facing business. Anyone planning to proceed with a project which will involve imports of any of the materials listed in schedule III must make application for approval of these imports on the basis of the project proposed. If the project is approved, all necessary imports under schedule III for it will be permitted.
On the other hand, as I mentioned, it was not necessary to make all conceivable imports for capital purposes subject to permit. By selecting a number of the key essentials, it was ensured that all projects of any significant magnitude would be brought to the department for review and approval.
It must be remembered in this connection that there are continuing domestic controls on steel and lumber. If permits are refused for a number of the essential key items, in the great majority of cases the project will have to be deferred and all the ancillary and minor imports of products not listed in schedule III which would have been made for it will automatically not be made.
While exactly the same procedure will be applied to imports from all countries, certain background facts must be taken into consideration. For example, during the war Canada was prevented from importing from the United

Kingdom as a result of the "essentiality program" of the United Kingdom itself. As a result, Canadian importers developed new sources and contacts, chiefly in the United States. This is a factor which must be taken into account in establishing regulations which will be equitable as between our two chief suppliers and customers.
The total value of imports from the United States of items listed in schedule III was $284 million in 1946, and on the basis of the first nine months of this year will be $445 million in 1947. Too much attention should not be paid to this figure, however, since on the one hand no estimate can be made of the proportion of this total which will be excluded because each case must be dealt with on it merits. On the other hand, as I have just explained, a large number of imports not listed will be automatically excluded by banning a few key materials essential to proceeding with a project.
A division to review applications and administer the issue of permits has been established in the department of which I am minister, under Mr. John Berry, who has been seconded from his position as president of War Assets Corporation. It is now actively functioning, and I need scarcely emphasize that all would-be importers of items listed in schedule III should be prepared to put before that division the details of their respective projects. Advisory industry committees are being set up-fof example, in steel and machine tools-following the practice of the war years. I put great stress on the importance of these committees: in this case our problem is their problem, and we intend to put the issue squarely before them. I am confident that, with the co-operation and understanding of business leaders, labour leaders, farmers, and consumers, we can, in Canada, weather any storm.
I must also mention a group of items included in schedule III scarcely less important than the key capital goods listed, but in a different category. This group includes automobiles and parts for the production of automobiles, and parts for the production-although not for the repair and servicing-of the durable consumer goods banned under schedule I. These include such products as washing machines, typewriters and domestic sewing machines. In other words, it is not proposed to permit the unlimited importation of parts for assembly in Canada of articles which are prohibited in their finished form, since this would clearly defeat the purpose of the ban as a measure for the conservation of United States dollars. A regulated volume of imports of such production parts for assembly in Canada will be allowed under permit, but only after the importer has satisfied the department

Foreign Exchange Conservation
that he is making every reasonable and practical effort to conserve United States exchange. In the case of automobiles and automobile production parts, which form the largest commodity in our adverse United States dollar balance of payments, arrangements will be worked out with the industry which, we hope, will achieve a substantial saving in exchange on a basis that will be equitable as between the different interests represented and which will accelerate the sound development of the industry in Canada.
While I have described the general administrative procedure to be followed, hon. members will naturally be interested in the principles which will guide this procedure. I should like to repeat that the guiding principle must be the conservation of United States dollars. Clear appreciation of this will avoid much misunderstanding. In other words, while our policy is, of necessity, restric-tionist in the sense of restricting our expenditures to our means, the approach is not protectionist. By "conservation of United States dollars" we mean a much more positive policy than simply replacing imports of finished goods from the United States with imports of parts for assembly in Canada. This alternative would also involve a heavy drain of United States dollars, and there are in this class a number of items of which Canadians must for a while get along with less. Our immediate necessity, and the objective which will have top priority in administration, is the expansion of sales in United States dollars. To this end the government intends to give energetic and effective encouragement to the development of our natural resources of mines, forests and fields which will find a market in the United States, and to the expansion of manufacturing industries that will be able to compete in the United States.
This is far from an uneconomic program, or one that must depend on protectionist restrictions. It is simply speeding up the established and natural development of the Canadian economy. I am interested to hear from hon. members opposite that we are "planning for recession", or for "a hunger program". Our wartime industrial experience showed that, with an adequate volume of production, Canadian unit costs and production performance compared favourable with the United States or with any other country in the world. It is our intention to provide for that adequate volume of production in every field in which it will be economically justifiable. We feel sure that the United States will accept the view that it is preferable to receive more Canadian goods which their consumers want than to lose much of their biggest market.
It is fortunate indeed that the Geneva agreement precedes our exchange difficulties. That agreement has greatly improved our potential for the long-run constructive correction of our chronic adverse balance with the United States. In my remarks to the house on the Geneva agreement last week I gave a number of examples of the spectacular development of our industry in the last eight years, and of the new opportunities which the agreement opens to us. At the same time I must say I know that the correction of our chronic United States dollar deficit will not be simple, and will not be accomplished without real effort.
In conclusion, I should like to emphasize that, dependent as we have been and are on many world conditions over which we have no control, Canada's policy to meet our present exchange problem will not be a defeatist and negative one. Some consumers, and some merchants, will be adversely affected in the short run. But we are going, aggressively, boldly and imaginatively, to develop Canadian resources and industry, and to find markets for those resources and industries which will provide us with additional United States dollars. Only by such action can we maintain, and stabilize, the highest standard of living which Canadians have yet achieved. And it is only in this way that we can maintain full employment, fair wages and a high level of income in Canada.
To sum up: 1. The basic solution of our dollar problem will be found in increased production.
2.	Short-term help will be sought by asking Canadians to consume less in order that Canada may export more.
3.	New production will be stimulated, particularly that production which is based on Canada's specialized resources.
4.	Present restrictionist policies are not intended to be protectionist. New industries based on such short-term policies will be discouraged. We will encourage new industries that have a place in Canada's normal competitive economy.
5.	Canada's basic materials, such as steel, must be used to best advantage. While low-cost housing and manufacturing capacity will be given high priority, construction projects that do not contribute to increased production will be discouraged.
6.	We will proceed with confidence in the belief that Canada can accomplish her national objective of safeguarding our national financial independence.
7.	This is every man's task and every Canadian will be expected to do his part.

Mr. DONALD M. FLEMING (Eglinton): Mr. Speaker, we have just heard from the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) an apologetic speech in support of the request of the government that he be vested with powers greater than any which have been vested in any person in Canada at any time in our history in peacetime, and perhaps in wartime also. The only person who gets anything out of this bill except austerity is the Minister of Reconstruction who is to get vast powers. Having lately come from the field of housing, fresh from the government's colossal failure there, the minister is now seeking to extend his rule and is inviting the house to assign to him new worlds to conquer. Perhaps it would not be amiss if I asked the minister, as I ask all others on the treasury benches who are similarly minded: upon what meat doth this our Caesar feed that he has grown so great? Apparently it is not on vegetables coming from the United States. We look upon the minister as the man who is to become under this legislation, if the house adopts it, the Canadian Cripps, the czar of Canada's economy.
It seemed to me that the principal reason given today by the minister in an effort to justify this extraordinary request for these amazing powers was that there would otherwise be a danger of inflation. I want to tell the minister and all members of the government that we have inflation today. It is past the incipient stage and the government's policy is responsible for it. I have here a statement from one of Canada's leading economists, Mr. Courtland Elliott. This gentleman commands the high regard of business. During the war he held a position with the government, functioning under the excess profits tax legislation. Speaking of the United States dollar scarcity in Canada, he said on November 11:
Conscious monetary and fiscal policy has increased our money supply in the hands of the public (from $2,876 million in 1939 to $7,476 million in 1947. Money burns holes in pockets and that means buying, and partly in the United States.

Foreign Exchange Conservation
The facts are crystal clear. The government is responsible for the situation we have today and for the great problem we face. It has been fiddling these many months while Rome burned. First, the problem has been open and obvious; it has not been a hidden problem.
Second, the problem did not develop overnight; it has been developing steadily and with increasing momentum.
Third, the problem began with the restoration to parity in the middle of 1946. The minister and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) invite this house to bury its intelligence and believe that was a pure matter of coincidence. No one will be fooled in that way. The beginning of the problem was in the middle of 1946.
Fourth, abundant warnings have been given to the government. Warnings were given last session in this chamber. I well remember the warnings of the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson), the hon. member for York South (Mr. Coekeram), and others. If the government wishes evidence of a more recent warning I would refer them to August 21 when the government of the United Kingdom suspended the free convertibility of sterling.
Fifth, this delay has meant a steady flight of dollars and decreased gold production. It has created a situation where the gold industry is literally fighting for its life. Eventually it was made the occasion for more drastic measures. Had action been taken long ago, other measures would have sufficed to cure this situation without a resort to this drastic program which the government has now announced.
Sixth, this government deliberately withheld information from parliament and from the Canadian people, information that should have been made available. I well remember, Mr. Speaker, in the standing committee on banking and commerce in the early part of the session in 1946, when we were considering the foreign exchange control bill, how we tried to get some information out of the government concerning the supply of United States dollars; and when the government took the step of restoring the dollar to parity with the United States dollar in the middle of 1946 how we tried to get some information; but we were deliberately and emphatically refused that information. In the intervening period the government has consistently hidden the facts. Apparently it was not prepared to trust parliament with the information.
Seventh, the remedy proposed by the government today is, stripped of all pretence,
dictatorship-nothing short of it. This is not the first time in history that an economic crisis or an economic problem has been made the occasion of a demand for dictatorial powers by someone, and it does not impress me in the least to hear the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) say in the house today, in defence of this request for these tremendous powers, "Oh, well, trust me." Every dictator-and we have had experience in the world these two past decades-has said that very thing when he asked for the first of the dictatorial powers with which he eventually was clothed.
Eighth, the measures that have been taken in keeping with this dictatorial remedy that has been proposed bear all evidences of having been conceived over-night. They are half-baked; they have been put together in haste. There is no excuse for that. The government have had ample warning of the situation. All these months they have known that measures would have to be taken. Surely they might at least have had a well prepared program to put forward. But what do we see? Here is the order in. council that was passed on the 12th day of.November and announced to the public in the last hour of the 17th day of November, P.C. 4678. And what happens? No sooner is the order in council made public than the necessity for amendments and changes immediately becomes apparent. On November 26 we have P.C. 4858 with the first batch of amendments. On December 8 the next one, P.C. 5017, and again the same day an announcement by the Minister of Finance of changes in the excise tax proposals; on December 1.1 a complete revision of the proposals with respect to the gold subsidy, and then another one w'hich has not been made public, but which in many respects reveals moie eloquently than do these other changes the colossal blunders that have been made.
Among the prohibitions contained in the government's announcement of November 17 was one applicable to the importation of western pine from the United States. This has been for a generation the principal source of material for sash and doors, and to some extent millwork, for the three prairie provinces and also the province of Ontario. Ninety per cent of the pine used by us for this purpose has come from the states of Washington, Oregon and1 northern California. That was shut out by this bureaucratic blunder of November 17. A knowledge of a little recent history would surely have taught the bureaucrats sitting on the government benches and elsewhere that during the war this staple necessity was so important that it was per-
Foreign Exchange Conservation

mitted to come in free. It was placed on the list of essential goods, and even the ten per cent import duty was taken off it during the wTar. But along came the bureaucrats with their blunders on November 17 and they shut it out. That situation persisted for some days. Now the government have changed it but they have not made any public announcement concerning the change.
The problem that we have before us today in all its critical proportions is a problem for which this government is responsible, and it will not be good enough for the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply today to put up a straw man in the form of inflation and knock him down to try to frighten the house with respect to inflation.
What wa9 put forward yesterday by the financial critic of the official opposition, my colleague the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell), was a proposal that we go back to the position where we were doing very well prior to the middle of 1946, the position in which stability had been achieved. There was not any suggestion about inflation, and I repeat that we have inflation today. This is a fine time now for the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply to be holding forth on the dangers of inflation, when he and his colleagues in the government are responsible for the inflation that exists in Canada today.
I do not need to remind the house that the government's announcements are full of contradictions. They appeared in the statements of the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply over the air and in the house; but I refer also to certain fundamental contradictions in government policy which have shown up so clearly in this situation. Time does not permit me to mention more than a fetw. They call for more freedom, but at the same time what they have been doing has been leading steadily to more and more restrictions. Second, they have been preaching stimulation of imports. They are those who preach that it is more blessed to import than to export; but what do we see today? Measures so drastic applied against imports into Canada that they have no parallel in our history.
Again they boast about the market far our wheat that they have obtained in the United States, and at the same time they tell farmers in this country that they will not be permitted to ship their wheat to that market. Then they boast about the way in which they have opened up the American market for Canadian beef cattle, and at the same time they continue to apply the embargo against the ship-

ment of beef cattle. These are fundamental contradictions in what the government have been doing before our very eyes; and last but by no means least, after they have been foisting on the Canadian people such a surfeit of talk and propaganda on the subject of our national prosperity, what do they bring us to now? Austerity, the tightening of our people's belts right across Canada by measures that will affect every man, woman and child in the country. Accompanying it all is again the usual contempt for parliament and parliamentary processes.
The reason for calling this session, as was announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on the 30th day of October, was the necessity for ratification of the Geneva trade agreements. Well, we have seen just how much there was in that pretext. There was nothing in it. And the Prime Minister on that occasion, as hon. members will see in the press reports, was asked by some representative of the fourth estate, "What about Canada's dollar crisis?" The Prime Minister was evasive on the subject, but when we got here the government claimed that parliament was called to discuss the dollar crisis. Apparently the reason for calling parliament underwent a transformation between October 30 and December 5. What do we see? In an act of condescension, the government that has shut off debate on one occasion in this house already, permits two days of discussion on this far-reaching measure, a gracious act of condescension. What does it all lead to? It leads to an adjournment tonight of the debate on this measure and we shall come back to it perhaps in February or March of next year. This is a sample of the urgency of the measures that prompted the government to call an emergency session of parliament, and the poppycock that has been offered to the house as to the reason why parliament was not called much earlier than this to deal with the dollar crisis and to deal effectively with it. The reason given is that it would not have been prudent for parliament to be in session while the negotiations were proceeding at Geneva. There are only two interpretations to be put upon that: one was that there were things that were not good for the representatives of other nations to know about us at Geneva; in other words, our negotiators were not telling them the whole story; and second, a distrust of parliament. These are the only two interpretations it is possible to put upon that statement.
Here we are today with this whole austerity program a fait accompli. You have it in effect today full and complete, and the government is apparently not in the least

worried if this debate is adjourned for a couple of months 'because it has its program in effect right now.
I have not the time to discuss order P.C. 4678 in detail now, but I point out in passing that it cuts across all existing contractual obligations even in cases where goods were paid for, even where they were moved into storage with a view t'o eventual movement to this country, and where no question of exchange was involved. In spite of that, the order cuts right across these obligations with the result that loss is entailed to Canadians even where no United States exchange was involved.
This order, P.C. 4678, is justified by the government under the terms of the Foreign Exchange Control Act of 1946. Let me remind you, Mr. Speaker, of what was said on this subject bv the then minister of finance when he was piloting the measure in t'he house. He said, at page 2547 of Hansard of 1946:
We have no intention of using this exchange control legislation to restrict anything but certain types of capital movement.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, we have the government today undertaking to justify P.C. 4678 on the strength of the Foreign Exchange Control Act of 1946. We have the government committing a complete, outright and deliberate breach of faith with parliament. What has happened is that parliament has been deceived as to the intention of the government with respect to this legislation. An opinion of the law officers of the crown has been referred to. I have the greatest respect for the law officers of the crown. I wish to make it clear that I would not be so bold or presumptuous as to set any opinion of mine against theirs; but it would be, I think, in a situation of this kind, extremely interesting for the house to see what that opinion is. In fairness to the house, the government ought to make public that opinion; it ought to bring it down in this house. We should know what the opinion of the law officers of the crown is upon which the government purport to justify this legislation.
If this legislation is valid, there was no occasion to bring the bill here; there was no occasion to bring parliament together to discuss this measure, and therefore the bill we are discussing is entirely unnecessary. I should like to know, in connection with that opinion, for instance, how it reconciles what has been done with subsection 2 of section 26 of the Foreign Exchange Control Act. In the preamble to P.C. 4678, one of the sections referred to as justifying or enabling the passing of that order in council is this section 26, 5849-26
which says in effect that no one shall import any goods into Canada except under a permit. Subsection 2 of section 26 has this to say:
The board shall not withhold a permit for the import of goods into Canada in any ease where the payment made or to be made therefor to a non-resident does not exceed the fair value thereof, and was made or is to be made in a currency designated by regulation as payable in connection with such a transaction.
If for no other reason than legitimate curiosity, one would like to know what that opinion of the law officers says about that section. One would like to know what the opinion says about that portion of the preamble to the Foreign Exchange Control Act which says "it is desirable to ensure that such reserves in foreign currency are used to promote and facilitate trade." They are being used under this measure today, under P.C. 4678, to restrict trade.
If this order in council is valid, why are we taking time to discuss Bill No. 3? Why, will you tell me, Mr. Speaker, have we in section 14 of the bill a provision which has the effect of making valid what has been done under the terms of P.C. 4678? There you have a provision which says in effect that P.C. 4678 is validated, with everything that has been done under it. Everything done under it is presumed to be valid and is confirmed by this legislation.
If the law officers of the crown had given the opinion which has been referred to, and if it justifies P.C. 4678, then we are being asked to legislate something that is quite unnecessary. In section 14 we are asked to do something that is completely unnecessary and therefore we are being asked to fan the air.
The Minister of Reconstruction today asked us not to think, with reference to the powers under this bill, in terms of dictatorship. It was a soothing kind of speech we heard from the minister today. I choose-I believe with much more realism and with a truer regard for the terms of the bill and of the order in council, P.C. 4678-to say that parliament is being asked to abdicate. That is what is involved in the bill. We might as well fold up as hand over to one minister powers of the breadth and scope contained in this Bill No. 3 and in P.C. 4678. It is not so many years ago that this chamber rang with the indignant protests and denunciations of the right hon. gentleman whose seventy-third birthday we have observed today. Back in 1934, dealing with a relatively simple and innocuous measure introduced by the government of that day,
Foreign Exchange Conservation

the right hon. gentleman fulminated in these words at ipage 2336 of Hansard of that year:
When the government believes it is in the interests of its own policies it may pass any order it pleases with regard to the trade of Canada, regardless of the legislation parliament itself has enacted or may enact.
Do hon. members (of the Commons) realize that this bill gives to the governor in council the power to prohibit absolutely the importation of goods from another country which the government may allege it is in the public interest to prohibit?
Those are the words the present Prime Minister uttered in 1934 on a bill which does not begin to compare even faintly with the bill that is before us today, in the scope of the powers that parliament is asked to confer in favour of one member of the government. Under this bill and under P.C. 4678, it is not one whit of exaggeration to say that the Minister of Reconstruction holds the Canadian economy in the hollow of his hand.
In these three schedules of the bill there is a list of commodities of tremendous proportions. There is no freedom left to business to decide what it is to purchase and what it is not to purchase. Apparently no thought was given to saying to any particular business, "We are going to restrict the amount of currency you can expend in the United States. We will see that certain things shall not be bought, but within the scope of the kind of things we show in the quota list, we will not interfere with your right of choice so long as you do not exceed the quota of currency to be made available to you". There is no thought given to that, and apparently it did not appeal to the government because the bill is designed to vest dictatorial powers in the hands of one man.
Gone are objective standards in the application of law to the citizens of the country, regardless of their walk of life or of their station. What the government has substituted is eventually the decision of one man. It is all in the minister's discretion, whatever is done under the act. The minister may be just as impartial, just as good as he today says he is. He may be all that; but there is no human being alive who, clothed with powers like these, will ever be able, human weakness being what it is, to divest himself completely of caprice and whim and favouritism and partisanship. It cannot be done. A great deal depends on the mood of the man at the time. I can well imagine coming before the minister for a permit on some occasions when his temper is good, when it might be easier to deal with him than on some other occasions when his temper is not so good, as we have seen in the house. For instance, I hope I am never in the posi-

tion of coming before the minister and asking him for the exercise of his discretion when he is in one of those moods where he is riding high and handsomely over the House of Commons.
Let us look at the terms of the bill itself. One does not need to go outside the terms of the bill itself to find the clear handwriting of those who believe that power should be absolute in the hands of the minister. In the debate on second reading I know it is not permissible to refer to the details of the bill, but I point out that power is given to the minister to suspend the operation of the act with regard to any person or class of goods. In other words, power is given to the minister to nullify the act completely if he chooses to do so. Not only that; but power is given to the minister, under another provision of this act, to move goods from one schedule to another. If he wishes, he can say, if it suits him, that goods included in schedule I shall be deemed to be included in schedules II and III.
Then let us remember this, Mr. Speaker. The fixing of the quotas with respect to those commodities enumerated in schedules II and III is vested in the minister and he is given complete and uncontrolled discretion with respect to them. Under P.C. 4678 the quotas are fixed. But under this bill there is no limitation on the power of the minister to fix the quotas. The minister can fix and unfix the quotas to his heart's content without ever going to anybody and seeking the power to do so. He has the power to do that. He can manhandle these quotas to his heart's content. Not only that, but what about the scheduled and non-scheduled countries? There is not a word in Bill No. 3 about scheduled and non-scheduled countries. P.C. 4678 divides the countries of the world into scheduled and non-scheduled countries. We have among the scheduled countries this enumeration: Cuba, the Dominican Republic, Guatemala, Haiti, Panama, El Salvador, Switzerland, the Union of Soviet. Socialist Republics, the United States of America and its possessions, and Venezuela. All other countries are deemed to be non-scheduled countries.
But what do we find under this bill? The minister can apply these import restrictions as he chooses without regard to the definition that exists today under P.C. 4678 with respect to scheduled and non-scheduled countries. If he wishes he can apply these restrictions to the hilt against our sister nations in the British commonwealth. There is no restriction in this bill with respect to scheduled and non-scheduled countries. In those respects, there is far less democracy in this bill than there was even under that dictatorial order in council P.C. 4678.

Then to cap all this, there is the provision in this bill that the burden of proof, with regard to anyone who is accused of violating the provisions of this act, is on the person charged with the violation. That is a fine sample of democracy, Mackenzie King government style, 1947.
Then the government has sought to beguile us with these choice promises as to the temporary nature of the measure; but the Minister of Finance gave it all away yesterday when he began on this note, that the scarcity of United States dollars in Canada is a permanent problem. The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, in his radio address, also talked about a long-term program to deal with a long-term problem, and also a short-term approach to the same problem. Yes, the problem is permanent. You will find, Mr. Speaker, that there is no time limit in this bill. There was a time limit imposed in the Foreign Exchange Control Act. But there is not any time limit in this bill. The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, in one of those suave, debonair, offhand statements' of his, says, in effect, "Well, when I say a matter of months, I really mean years." He said that yesterday, that a matter of months does not mean something under a year, it means more than a year; that means years. By this curious process of sophistry in which the minister excelled today, yesterday and on November 20, he has somehow persuaded himself and asked the house to believe that a month is a year, that one-twelfth equals one-it sounds very much like his reports on housing-and apparently he has persuaded himself that the lesser includes the greater, as a mathematical proposition. Apparently somebody has been talking to the minister since he made that radio address on November 20. Apparently somebody has drawn to his attention the fact that it was a silly statement he made when he said this problem could be cleared up in a matter of months.
Having regard to the blunder of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply and a similar blunder of the Minister of Finance who denied in the house last week that he had ever used the word "austerity" and then on the next day had to read an extract from his own radio speech of November 17 in which that very word appears, I suggest that these two ministers are eligible for a leading place on a feature program of a Canadian radio station. The name of the program is, " Did I say that?"
They said this would be a temporary measure. The Geneva agreements, which they are nullifying by this measure, will last only three years. Will anybody guarantee that this measure will not nullify the Geneva trade agreements for their full three-year life?

While we are on the matter of months, may I say that today marks the end of one month since the great radio speech of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance on November 17, and look at what has happened in the matter of one month.
One of the features of this legislation which ought to provoke the strongest opposition in this house is that, although our problem is purely and simply a scarcity of United States dollars, these restrictions are not limited in their effect to imports from the United States. They apply to imports from other countries as well, including many countries with which we have a favourable trade balance, to which we are selling much more than we buy and from which we should be encouraging imports today, in order to help them on the road to recovery.
At page 222 of Hansard, Mr. Speaker, you will recall that my esteemed leader drew the attention of the Minister of Finance to a considerable list of items which the government of the United Kingdom had indicated that that nation was in a position to supply in the export market during this year. As will be found at page 222, the Minister of Finance said:
May I say that the embargoes contained in the bill now before the house do not materially affect exports from the United Kingdom.
That statement made by the Minister of Finance cannot be reconciled with the facts. An analysis has been made-I do not take personal credit for it-of eighty-six items in that list which was referred to by the leader of the opposition; and of the eighty-six, what do we find? Thirty-nine of them are now banned from entering Canada; thirteen are restricted by quotas, and twenty-one are subject to the twenty-five per cent excise tax.
