Mr. Speaker, I find it impossible to dissociate the present economic crisis from the war. For five or six years we used all our resources of every type to smash Europe, politically, socially and materially. It will take us a good deal more than five years to rebuild the damage we have done, because Europe must be rebuilt for our own sakes, lor there lie some of our very best markets. And so the cost of reconstruction, I maintain, is part of the cost of war.
However, there is another cost, an intangible cost, the cost in ideas-cherished ideas which perhaps will have to go overboard because they are at variance now with the facts of the situation.
I hope the government has paid that price, because the problems which confront us today cannot be met with habits of mind which could not cope with the trade depression. It has been said by many speakers that the crisis has been coming for some time and that everybody knew it. Two years ago in the annual report of the foreign exchange control board, it was forecast to some extent. I will grant that perhaps the situation has not been aided by restoration to parity of our dollar.
When the announcement about parity was made in the house I accepted it, as I still do; and I do not want to get into any argument about it. But I would say this, that so far as devaluation is concerned, it will hurt everybody in Canada. The government has taken another alternative in selecting certain items which will be prohibited or else put on a quota. I doubt very much, however, if the
Foreign Exchange Conservation

group of nations has agreed to take discriminatory action against all if it has taken it against one-then if it is compelled to take action against one, all the others must suffer. The effect of the non-discriminatory clause is to restrict trade. Contrary to what the minister thinks, we do not increase world trade; rather we restrict it.
Apparently this non-discrimination clause is in operation due to what the Minister of Finance called an American fetish. Has the government of Canada abdicated in favour of American fetishes? Personally I object to that type of American domination. The leader of this party, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), has told us that trade between Canada and the United States is competitive. He has urged upon the house that our export trade should lie with what the Minister of Reconstruction calls our historic markets, the United Kingdom and Europe. Instead, the government is going ahead with efforts to integrate our industries with United States industries.
What exactly does that mean? Does that mean that we are to make parts for United States manufactured goods? Does it mean the rationalization of industry in the sense that we make articles of a certain type for this continent while the United States makes others? Does it mean that we in Canada are to become hewers of wood and drawers of water for United States industrialists by sending them our natural resources, while they fabricate them and send them back to us in the form of manufactured articles? Does it mean the merging of ourselves with the United States economy so that we become an economic colony? If it means any or all of these things, it means putting ourselves in a position where we will suffer from every blunder in United States policy. It means that we will suffer from any booms or depressions which they may have in their economy.
It has been suggested that perhaps Canada will be the Belgium of the new world, but I do not think that is the case. It looks as though we are the Czechoslovakia of North America; we are to become the prisoners of dollar imperialism. Fifty years ago there were Americans who were afraid that humanity would be crucified on a cross of gold. IV e need not be afraid of that now because we are finally hooked on the talons of the double eagle. In effect what the government has done is to abrogate Canadian sovereignty.
I am not going to traverse the ground already covered by members of our group. They have stated our case on the excise fax

and on monopolies. However, I should like to direct the attention of the government to the situation with regard to prices in this country. A measure such as this will increase prices to the working people and farmers of Canada. If such a plan is carried out it will have serious social consequences to this country. It is something we have to guard against.
I maintain that the effect of this bill unaccompanied by controls will be to make scarcity more abundant, to deny to those who lack the money the ability to buy goods which are available only to the wealthy, and to make certain that discrimination against our own people which the government professes to find so offensive when directed against the United States. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny):
That all the words after the word "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"this bill be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house price ceilings should be imposed immediately on all goods or products of any class or kind the importation of which is prevented or limited by embargoes or restrictions."

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although I realize that the time for this debate is short, yet I am urged to participate in it because from the time the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) made his announcement on November 17 last on the Geneva trade agreements and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) immediately afterwards made public this country's emergency program to correct our trade balances, I felt keenly that nothing could be more important to the people of this nation than that we realize 'the advantages as well as the difficulties contained in both the long-term and short-term programs.
There is nio doubt in my mind that the agreements reached at Geneva constitute the most advanced plan of removal of international trade barriers that any group of nations have been able to agree upon to date. The accomplishment of this agreement reflects great credit on the Canadian representation at that meeting, as it also reflects great credit on those from other nations. Nothing as far-seeing could have been possible except from the minds and brains of mein with broad vision and the knowledge that in this course lay the hope of a peaceful world.
I also feel most keenly that it is essential for us to keep these two programs, one domestic, the other international, in proper perspective. We must guard against the temptation to look upon the immediate as the more important and, because of that attitude, forget that the restrictive part of the one may, in our particular case, 'be but a stepping-stone to great opportunities inherent in the other.
However, important as was the statement of the Prime Minister, and grateful as we were to hear his voice on that occasion, the statement of the Minister of Finance brought such a complete realization of Canada's United States dollar position that it was only natural that the scope of the Canadian program should receive the greater consideration, and that the plan should become today's outstanding problem.
For years we Canadians have been buying more than we were selling in the United States. At the same time we have been selling more than we were buying from Europe and the rest of the world, but we were able to balance our United States dollars by the use of the moneys that we received from Europe and the rest of the world.
At the end of the war came also the end of the lend-lease program, the end of the Hyde Park agreement, which I am afraid most Canadian people have not yet realized the full benefits of. It also brought to us the necessity
of aid to Europe and constantly higher loans. It also brought a complete new condition for Canadians. What Canadians found previously difficult to understand they now understand completely. They understand that foreign exchange is not a matter for bankers, but it is a matter for the individual Canadian, and we are all concerned in it. Had we made no loan to Europe in 1946, and had Europe been able to get United States dollars for their purchases we would now have an increased rather than an almost exhausted trade balance. Of course we had no obligation, other than a moral one, to make a loan, but to make a loan was human, honourable and in our own interest the best thing to do.
But let us assume just for a moment that we had refused to face up to these changed world conditions. What would we now be doing? There would be no so-called austerity program. Canadian pleasure travel to the United States would be unrestricted. We could buy our luxuries, new motorcars, washing machines, radios, refrigerators. Canada would not need to work at the menial task of growing its own cabbage, lettuce, tomatoes, early potatoes and, in fact, some late ones as well. We would be having a perfectly enjoyable and lovely time, but unfortunately our happy time would sooner or later have to come to an end. It would have ended abruptly when our resources had been depleted, had we no longer had the power to make ourselves self-supporting. Here, let me say, I do not refer only to our dollar balance in the United States; I refer also to the natural resources of this country, which we would have been depleting, exporting to foreign countries in order to get the exchange to pay for goods bought in the United States. Fortunately for us, the Minister of Finance had the courage to place the complete picture, without hesitation, before the people of Canada. Any less strong pronouncement of these facts would not have brought us to a full realization of our position.
Let us not regard this entire development as an insurmountable hurdle, but as a situation in which our real ability and ingenuity shall be brought into play in facing up to the changing circumstances. It is fortunate for us that it has happened at a time when our neighbours will in many cases, I am sure, welcome the Canadian move to look after our own needs, to take some of the strain off their own short supply of material as well as food. Save for some interested groups who have been shipping to us, the move will not be misunderstood.
As the result of our unbalanced trade with the United States, Canada is like a person who is quickly using up all savings to make current
Foreign Exchange Conservation

purchases. When those savings have run out, then what? That specifically is the major and immediate economic challenge which we shall be called upon to meet and solve. The question is in the minds of all serious thinking Canadians who feel, and I think rightly, that all things should be done to keep this country from even verging on a condition which in the minds of other people, particularly in the United States, would place us in the category of a dependent nation. No one in Canada, and I doubt whether many in the United States, would want to feel that Canada was a United States problem.
The short-term section of our program, with its import restrictions, its gold bonus, the United States loan, the limitations on pleasure travel, is, in my opinion, a stop-gap action to achieve immediate results. The method through which we shall finally meet our problem brings up the real challenge to Canadian ingenuity and resourcefulness. I should like to divide it into two main activities-production and salesmanship, or production and merchandising if you prefer it.
I feel that Canadians are not really good merchandisers, and that the Canadian people have not a great deal of resistance ability against the merchandising abilities of some other people. This course involves comprehensive, long-term planning, and it also involves a real consciousness on the part of Canadian industry and business, that its position and its methods must come under careful, self-imposed scrutiny if it is to expand or even to retain the present domestic market, or if it is to compete successfully with merchandising and production methods adopted by competitive countries.
In discussing this question, I should like to emphasize that there is not the slightest intention of implying that we can live without trade with other countries, including the United States. I wish to emphasize, however, that trade must be two-way in every sense of the word, and our present position is far from that. Last year Canada bought seventy-five per cent of its imports from the United States, but sold back to the United States only thirty-nine per cent of its exports.
When we look critically at the total score of our indebtedness to the United States for the purchase of goods for Canadian consumption we can readily see that it is made up of many thousands of items covering a wide range of categories; in fact, almost every major industrial field as well as a great many agricultural products.
As an example, and only as an example, listed among these many items are such things

as lettuce, corn, tomatoes, spinach, celery and many dozens of similar items, both fresh and canned or otherwise processed. Their total costs run into millions of dollars, and that expenditure is actually for those commodities which I feel, with some planning, could be supplied almost entirely from domestic production.
It seems staggering to find that during the first seven months of 1947 Canada's bill for the importation of cabbage alone was only slightly short of 81,000,000. Surely something could be done right here in Canada to improve a situation of that kind. These few things I have mentioned are but a small fraction of the total imports of that kind and do not include any of the imports which, either because of climate or because of other factors, this country could not hope to produce successfully, such as a number of citrus and tropical fruits.
But even in those fields where we have rather indolently accepted the idea that the only place in which to 'buy is the United States, I am thoroughly convinced that tremendous improvements can be made if we waken up to the possibilities of doing something for ourselves. It is up to us to do a better job of salesmanship and to encourage originality in design, and it is up to us to throw overboard our own demands for quick and exorbitant profits.
The effectiveness of the selling campaign which made California "Sunkist" oranges almost a byword, both in the United States and in Canadian homes, is generally recognized, and a knowledge of its effects on the California orange industry is common property. But if we in Canada used that knowledge in taking a similar course of action with some of our own products, such as, for example, fortified apple juice, especially graded potatoes and many other things, we could achieve similar results. I have mentioned potatoes several times because I remember that during the war and before the war we could go and buy Utah potatoes on this market. They were specially graded and temptingly put up, and a lady could go and buy one potato, take it to her apartment, bake it and have supper for two. We have just as good potatoes in the east, in the west and in the middle west, but we did not have the foresight or the courage to go about dealing with them in the same way. That is what I am trying to emphasize. It is a matter of production, but it is equally a matter of good salesmanship practice.

I have used that simply to illustrate a situation which I think is quite typical of our whole production and merchandising program. 1 have mentioned some food items which are part of our billion dollar bill. But the food1 bill is not by any means the one in which we add up the greatest number of dollars on the red side of the ledger. Take a look at the really big field which accounts for more than a third of our drain of United States dollars, iron and its products. Listed among the thousands of items are such things as pipe fittings, for which we paid almost $1,000,000 in the first seven months of this year. In the same period, wire for the manufacture of wire rope cost us about one and a quarter million dollars. Automobile engines sent the bill up another four and a half million dollars. .Plows and plow parts account for more than two million dollars. Logging machinery used in one of Canada's most permanent industries added another three million dollars. As in the categories previously mentioned, these are just a few examples making up the list which includes everything from tank cars to fingernail files; and the last item, incidentally,, accounted for almost $20,000 in the first seven months of this year. We paid $300,000 for fishing rods imported from the United States. Surely one cannot call that an austerity program, when we are asked to produce our own fingernail files and1 our own fishing rods rather than having to buy them from some place else.
In the field of wood and paper products we find another long list of items which, it seems to me, could be produced in this country without too much trouble and with satisfactory profits to the makers. Just one or two examples occurred to me on looking over the list of imports. I find that we spent during the first seven months of this year about a quarter of a million dollars for railway ties, which were referred to last night by the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith). We spent another $150,000 for telegraph poles and piling and a further $200,000 for cedar lumber. But I could go on almost indefinitely giving examples such as those I have already mentioned. While it may appear that the individual amounts are not great, in the aggregate they add up to that billion dollar six-months bill which was met by less than half out of current earnings by this country of United States dollars, the remainder from savings.
It seems to me almost unbelievable that we in Canada are unable to meet such things as style requirements or other quality requisites, particularly when we know that Canadian manufacturers have already gained an enviable reputation in many countries as a result of the fine job they have done in turning out excellent quality in many lines. We have too readily adopted ready-made quality and style standards. It may be the easy way; but it is, in my opinion, unimaginative and lacking initiative to such an extent that it stifles any creative ability which might find truly Canadian expression in fashion or quality of Canadian-made goods.
The same sort of attitude has developed with respect to our buying habits. It is quite conceivable, in my. opinion, that thousands of materials could be purchased by Canadian industry from sources other than in United States, probably at no greater cost and with the added advantage of making contacts where Canadian goods could be marketed. But because it is just a bit less trouble to get on the telephone and call New York, or some other United States city, we have failed to expand1 our activities in that connection to the extent which we could have done. I think there is some excuse for Canadians falling into that habit. It is three thousand miles from one coast to the other; but it is only three or four, maybe twenty miles across to a large city to the south of us where we can get what we want over-night. Surely we are not in such a hurry for most of these things that we in the west could not afford to call up Toronto and Montreal, not forgetting that there is Vancouver and Victoria as well.

In my opinion, the responsibility for taking action along this line rests squarely upon the shoulders of the main divisions of our industrial and financial structures, just as long as we retain the idea that the free enterprise system can do an effective job. That freedom also involves a responsibility, and that responsibility includes much more than mere selfish interest which, through its failure to recognize the national interest, becomes in time a threat to the welfare of individuals and industries alike. Governments in a more or less free economy can be a very real help to private business in providing a kind of clearing house for ideas and in paving the way through legislative action or to some extent through research. But, I repeat, the final responsibility rests with the industries themselves.
Personally, I am in favour of retaining a small section of the wartime prices and trade

board to give some leadership in aotion to improve some of our production methods. A number of the staff of the board gained, during the war, some valuable experience in that field; and I feel they would be extremely useful as a permanent co-ordinating body. Then in the merchandising field, I feel quite strongly that some section of the Department of Trade and Commerce should be in a position to give sound advice to industry and business and should carry out continuous research in selling programs.
I have given these few suggestions to show the nature of the problem that we in Canada must come to grips with.' I want to emphasize the fact that there is a short-term and longterm viewpoint we must achieve. I want, most of all, to point out the necessity, certainly not the impossibility, of finding the answer to this problem.
I have mentioned a number of items, using them as examples to show some of the possibilities open to us in helping to get ourselves out of some of the immediate difficulties as far as United States dollars are concerned. The items I have mentioned are those which we have been importing, but our list of imported goods is not by any means the most important. There are thousands of other manufactures which could be developed in this country that would add to our sales to the United States. I think Canadians have been far too much inclined to look upon a log as a finished product rather than as a raw material which we ourselves could puit through all the various processes required to make it acceptable consumer goods for sale both on the domestic market and for export. Here again I spoke only of a log for the purpose of illustrating what I mean. All our raw material is in the same position.
The extent to which we change our attitude and practice in this regard will decide, in the long ran, the extent to which we may, as soon as possible, return to more normal trade with our southern neighbour and the extent to which we may import the thousands of articles which, because of climatic or other reasons, are more efficiently or profitably produced in the United States.
A full program of development in Canada, industrially and agriculturally, must mean, if it is to be a success, an immigration policy based on careful selection, with the need of maintaining a virile, healthy Canada. An expanding population of virile people on this part of the continent cannot be anything but to the general advantage of the United States, as we shall still be dependent upon them for the things we are unable to produce. The difference in climate makes it possible for us

to have an integrated, complementary trade with the United States, in many respects, without affecting our commonwealth relations.
At the present time we hold an important place in international affairs. Our present commitments are, I think, about our limit. The world thinks of us as a people who believe in fair play. Our history justifies this thought. The best assurance that we can play our part in the international scene is for us to develop our own country and keep it vigorous and strong, economically and socially. Industrial Canada does not mean, as I see it, a few great industries in a few large cities. It means an industrial people working with intelligence and diligence to develop those things which nature has so bountifully bestowed upon us.

Mr. Speaker, on this day of bouquets, possibly it would not be amiss, as far as this bill is concerned, if an austerity bouquet were offered at this time. Having listened to the address, not only of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), but also of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe), in which each endeavoured to justify the necessity of the bill before the house, I intend to vote against it.
Over a very considerable period of time I have believed that this government is following 'the road of dictatorship in this country, and it is of interest to know that in a book which has been referred to on a number of occasions in this house, namely the monumental work by Hayek "The Road to Serfdom", there is a reference to what takes place in a nation where there is foreign exchange control. Let me quote from the footnote at page 92, wherein there is set out the situation with reference to foreign exchange control and what it leads to:
The extent of the control over all life that economic control confers is nowhere better illustrated than in the field of foreign exchanges. Nothing would at first seem to affect private life less than a state control of the dealings in foreign exchange, and most people will regard its introduction with complete indifference. Yet the experience of most continental countries has taught thoughtful people to regard this step as the decisive advance on the path to totalitarianism and the suppression of individual liberty. It is, in fact, the complete delivery of the individual to the tyranny of the state, the final suppression of all means of escape-not merely for the rich but for everybody. Once the individual is no longer free to travel, no longer free to buy foreign books or journals, once all the means of foreign contact can be restricted to those of whom official opinion approves or for whom it is regarded as necessary, the effective control of opinion is much greater than that ever exercised by any of the absolutist governments of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.
In the explanation by the minister as to what he intended to do when he secured these powers under the bill, he stated, in effect, that "its guiding principle will be the restriction of the use of United States dollars."
The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), in a powerful indictment of the government, bore out what Hayek says in this book, namely, that control over exchange is, in fact, the road to totalitarianism and dictatorship. What is the position of the minister to be? He makes no excuses for the power he is going to exercise, a power the like of which, as the hon. member for Eglinton said today, has never before been asked for anywhere by any government in any democracy at any time. Imagine what it means to freedom in this country when, in the hands of the Minister of Reconstruction, without any appeal, the right will rest to command, to countermand, to browbeat and to intimidate, if he will, every businessman in Canada!	,

It transforms him into the people's master; and if parliament passes this legislation in its present form, parliament will, in fact, give to the minister immunity from challenge, recause that is what we are doing. We say ;o him in effect, "You exercise this power as you will, with freedom from scrutiny, however unfair, . however politically biased the decision may be".
I have asked this question and no minister has endeavoured to answer it yet: When has any government asked that any of its ministers shall, in fact, be the master, the judge and executioner of business or of individuals in our country? Equality before the law, which is the essence of freedom, the essence of the right to live, is denied, and there is placed in the hands of the minister the power to declare who shall, in fact, survive in business and who shall, in fact, die as a result of his edicts and his ukases. I do not over-state the case, and in support I know of no better editorial on the subject than that which appeared in the Western Producer of Thursday, December 4, 1947. This paper for years has taken the stand that there has been no danger in this country of any government endeavouring to take unto itself powers of dictatorship. But what did this paper say in its editorial under the caption, "Canada a Dictatorship"? This is what it states:
The charge of dictatorship has often been flung at the present Ottawa regime but most Canadians do not take it seriously. They find it hard to credit that any government elected by democratic processes, and never backward in proclaiming its loyalty to democratic principles would, to any serious extent, deviate from its professions. Yet many who have closely followed the course pursued by the federal government during the last decade have discerned some definite and quite disturbing developments.
It deals at length with the statement of the Minister of Finance in his radio speech of November 17, and then it says:
For surely, assuming that any standards of honour and decency remain, if parliament did not know it was voting these powers-

The powers of the foreign exchange control board which the Minister of Finance admits he did not know he possessed.
-and the government did not know it was receiving them they were never given nor received. This is the kind of subterfuge used by a responsible minister to avoid the necessity of consulting with the duly elected representatives of the people. Perhaps it is time that we took the charge of dictatorship more seriously.
Read that order in council to which the minister referred1 today, P.C. 4678; ascertain the powers that are contained therein, an order in council which will be continued in existence, and let anyone rise in his place and say that that order in council does not confer upon a minister of the crown a power with respect to which that minister is responsible neither to parliament nor to the courts of the country.
Did something happen on November 17 that made it necessary for this government to depart from the time-honoured procedure of having parliament called together for the purpose of having budget proposals presented in a legal and constitutional form? From what the minister said yesterday, it is clear that the foreign exchange problem has been continuing month by month. The government knew of its existence and1, as the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) said, it just waited, hoping that something would turn up. Ministers travelled in all parts of the world at the time when conditions were most serious and when exchange was being lost in a way that held danger for the economy of the people of Canada. Then finally, on November 17, without any reason whatsoever for fixing that date, parliament was deliberately flouted by the actions of the government in giving instructions to officers of the Department of National Revenue that on and after said date they were to do certain things which had1 never been before parliament and had never been considered by parliament.

I say to my hon. friends in the government of this country, that by that action they committed a crime against constitutional government in this country. And they wish us to act as rubber-

Some people say to me that private enterprise is on trial; rather it is a planned economy that is on trial, because for the last year and a half the foreign exchange control board has had the power to prevent the exchange crisis. This afternoon my right hon. friend said, in effect, that the government named the tariff items, by numbers. It is quite simple; read the schedules. To illustrate, in the first list it was prohibited to import diamonds. Then it was found that diamonds included commercial diamonds. So they had to say the prohibition did not cover commercial diamonds, and .finally they had to remove diamonds from the list. And so it goes. I have item after item before me of like kind, a kind of put-and-take proposition, a kind of trial and error proposition. There are commodities included, too, where it was found its result was to keep out things from Britain or from France, and the officials had to make changes accordingly because they did not want that to happen. So day to day confusion becomes more confusing.
Some say no political considerations will enter into this matter. Tell that to the businessmen across this country. They will come to members of parliament and say that ruination faces them. Then they speak of the possible unemployment that is going to result, the undermining of their business and the alteration of their economy. You ask them, "May I use your name and point out the example?" What is the answer? "Oh, no; we dare not." All across this country today the psychology of fear has gripped businessmen. They are fearful lest by representation they in any way incur the wrath of him who, after all, has the right to say whether or not they shall survive.
Parliament should remove from business the shackles that a muddled tyranny has already imposed upon it in a matter of three or four weeks. I believe the speech made last evening by the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) was a real contribution. I believe the policy of this government is one of defeatism, though today the Minister of Reconstruction said it was not. It is a policy of defeatism, pessimism and fear. Let us encourage young men to have their own businesses in this country. According to a Gallup poll, seventy-four per cent of our people want to do business for themselves. The hired man wants to be a farmer, the prospector wants to be a mine owner; the worker wants to be the owner of a business. This austerity program denies the opportunity to develop small business. It paralyses the little businessman, the small manufacturer who has built up his business in the last two or three years. The veteran who came back from overseas, whose business depends upon the importation

of small parts which he assembles in this country, finds that under this austerity program he is denied the right to live.
Mr. Speaker, we have a challenge in this country. We see our young men going across the boundary line. Some say private enterprise here holds out no promise to young men. Why is it that last year 30,000 went across to the United States? They went to the greatest country in the world that believes in private enterprise, in order to have an opportunity they consider is denied them in Canada. Let us in this parliament endeavour to build up a desire on the part of our people, encouraged by the government, encouraged 'by leadership in this country, to develop the eighty-five per cent of Canada that is yet undeveloped. You say to me that we have a Department of Mines and Resources. That is so; and what are the figures in connection with that department? Last year the total amount expended in connection with our natural resources amounted to only sixty cents out of every $100 spent. Let us expand. Let us develop. At this itime, when Canada should be developing, let us not place upon the initiative of men prepared to take a chance in business the shackles of the muddling tyranny of governmental authority.
Someone may say that business is not frightened. Have you heard from our businessmen how they feel about it? Have they any assurance as to what the law will be tomorrow, as to what changes will be made tomorrow by the minister? Unless there is reasonable assurance for the immediate future, initiative is denied. You deny that freedom to which Burke referred 170 years ago:
Our constitution is like our island, which uses and restrains its subject sea; in vain the waves roar. In that constitution, I know, and exultingly I feel, both that I am free, and that I am not free dangerously to myself or to others. I know that no power on earth, acting as I ought to do, can touch my life, my liberty, or my property. I have that inward and dignified consciousness of my own security and independence, which constitutes, and is the only thing which does constitute, the proud and comfortable sentiment of freedom in the human breast . . .
Can the spirit of freedom in the human breast live when parliament is asked to give a minister the power to grant freedom to one and dispense tyranny to another? Is there freedom in a country where, at a time when there should be development, the government takes a stand for restriction; when there should be expansion, it raises the flag of control? I admit that the minister has great ability, and I am not making light of it. But since the government has seen fit to decontrol the economy, the minister has been playing a hand that will get this country into greater difficulties.
I object to the non-discrimination section in this bill. It is, of course, a logical development from the government's attitude and support of the Geneva trade pacts. In carrying out the non-discrimination section, when ve protect ourselves by putting up discriminatory provisions against the United States we are also forced to impose discrimination against all other nations.
In the past we have never had a balance with the United States, and I believe it is foolishness to suggest that we can have a balance in the foreseeable future, under multilateral trade. In other words, if this unbalanced condition continues it will become greater and greater; more and more restrictions will have to be imposed. And as we impose more and more restrictions against the United States, so we are forced to impose more and more restrictions against the rest of the world. In other words, the government's free trade policy will turn into its opposite, so that we shall be going into a complete state of isolation.
There have been attempts by several speakers, from both the Liberal side and the Tory side, to turn this debate along the lines of protection versus free trade; tariffs versus free trade. That attitude in this day and age reminds me of the totem poles for which my district is famous-monuments to a colourful but bygone age, and fit only for museum pieces.
The struggle in the world markets today is not between those who believe in high or low tariffs. The struggle today is between multilateral trade and bilateral trade. Bilateral trade is that means of trading which brings about a balance between nations, without the intervention of currency-or hard currency, as it is known. It is much like the trade agreement which was published the other day between Great Britain and the U.S.S.R. The

statement was made that no hard currency was considered in that trade; all balances would be settled in goods.
Therefore we find that multilateral trade is slowly but surely coming to a dead stop. We find) such countries as Sweden curtailing imports from the United States; we find Canada doing the same thing, and Great Britain also. Why? Because they have no United States dollars. Under multilateral trading, wherever an unbalance exists as specified under the Bretton Woods agreement it must be settled in United States dollars or gold. No country has United States dollars or gold. The government is saying to us: You are not allowed to carry on a friendly poker game in your own home; you must go and play in a professional layout. When you get into such an institution the house takes a rake-off on every pot. Every gambler knows that if you stay long enough the house will take your whole stake. That is what has actually happened. Two years ago we had a billion and a half dollars; now we are going to the house and asking for another $300 million. Any gambler also knows that if he carried on under that method he would wind up being a swamper in the institution with the job of sweeping up the cigarette butts and other junk. That is the position in which every Canadian is going to find himself. He will find himself faced with the high cost of living of the United States worker without in turn receiving his high wages. We are to be peons of Wall Street.
The government's attitude toward the United States is, to say the least, subservient. In discussing the non-discrimination clause several days ago, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) said that it was a fetish with 'he United States. Therefore, even though it is a detriment to Canada, we must abide by it. In the last year or so we have read in our press of agreements between Russia, Roumania, Yugoslavia and Poland; there has been much reference to the domination of those nations by the U.S.S.R., and it has been said that the governments of those countries were just stooge governments. What is this government? It is nothing more than that. Seemingly the marrow has leaked out of the bones of the men on that side of the house. Either that, or the United States has taken a leaf out of recent history and planted a fifth column in the ranks of the government for the creation of another banana republic; but instead of being even a banana republic, we are to be just hewers of wood and drawers of water.

The answer is as I gave it a moment ago. At that time the purchasing power of the Canadian dollar was below that of the United States dollar, and the Canadian dollar was pegged deliberately at that level at a time which closely coincided with the almost complete closing of the border to travel and trade, so that we might conserve currency in order to buy war materials. That situation continued until it was eased in consequence of the Hyde Park agreement of April, 1941.
In the course of his remarks the other night, the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell)

said, "something is wrong", that when a number of countries were cutting down their purchases, that somebody must be making a profit. He went on to suggest that it was a bad course for us to be following, that we should sell our wealth abroad in order to maintain our own economy.
I quite agree with the hon. member when he says that something is wrong. The fact is that the world has not yet nearly recovered from the most devastating war in history, a war which lasted six years. Most of the countries of Europe have been over-run by the enemy. Old channels of trade and old standards have been destroyed. The whole western coast of the Pacific, almost the whole continent of Asia, is in a turmoil, and simultaneously with this we find a very large section of Europe and Asia divided by an iron curtain which helps to prevent recovery. At the same time we see the greatest and most powerful nation in the world with a large productive capacity needed abroad, but which other countries cannot buy because they have not the means with which to pay.
That, I suggest, is something wrong; and for a country like Canada, dependent as it is on world trade to a greater degree than any other nation, it is a situation which leads to serious consequences. Hon. members are aware, and the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario admitted, that we had done a great deal by way of gifts to Britain. If I might recall the figures, there was a gift in 1942 of one billion dollars; there was, during the war, $2,161 million in mutual aid; there was a loan in 1946 of $1,250 million; there was the consolidation of the old loan of $700 million; and, in addition, there was the fact that very large supplies of food, larger, I believe, than any other country shipped, were shipped to Britain, some of them at prices below world prices. That meant, as we all know, that Canada did more to help Britain than any other country in proportion to population.

I got these quotations; and after I said, "Thank you," the final word was, "Please be sure and don't say where you got the information." What difference on earth could it make? Only this, that this house, like practically every other financial house in the country, does a certain amount of dealing in bondls with the Bank of Canada. They are beholden to the Bank of Canada. Certainly, since the war years every chartered bank has felt itself so beholden to the Bank of Canada that the officers of those banks are afraid to open their mouths and say what they think, because the Bank of Canada can. make it either difficult or easy for them. So they are very much afraid of saying what is on their minds. That is what happens when we put power into the hands of a government which does not merely lay down the rules under which business shall be conducted, but actually conducts the business itself, and has the power of life and death.
Now, sir, if I' may turn, in the few minutes remaining to me, to the subject of this debate-

May I say that in the remarks which I shall make I would not for one moment presume to have the inexhaustible confidence which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has in the opinions he gives forth to the house; nor would I hope to fall into the same fallacious economic theory which we heard from the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply here today.
The situation is that in dealing with these very broad economic questions, no one really knows exactly what the answer is. There are certain indications, however, as to what the proper course should be, and I should like to put forward those indications, as I see them. Even the Minister of Finance admitted that the government's advisers were not infallible-and that was indeed a very great admission for him to make. But we are facing a grave issue. Andi the minister admitted that when the decision was made on July 5, 1946, to revalue our dollar to parity with the United States dollar, the basis for the government's reasoning turned out to be wrong. Yet the decision remained correct, according to the government.
What were some of the reasons which in July, 1946, the government relied upon when it brought the Canadian dollar up to parity with the United States dollar? First of all, it thought international trade would expand, that there would be more sterling convertible into dollars. That did not turn out to be the case. Second, the government thought Canadian imports from the United States would level off; exactly the reverse happened. Third, the government thought prices, after the lapse of the office of price administration in. the United States, would go up in that country and then they would come down. Quite the reverse has happened. Prices in the United States continue to go up, and indications are that for the months ahead they will continue to rise.
Are the advisers of the government therefore any more likely to be right now than they were in July, 1946? The human equation in these economic questions is incalculable, particularly in a free society; and recent events indicate that the human equation is just about as uncertain in the soviet society.
I believe every businessman would now consider that the action on July 5, 1946, of the government was a mistake. The old purchasing power parity theory of exchange which, was connected with the gold standard has disappeared. Under it, if costs in one country became lower than in. another country, the country with the higher costs naturally bought where costs were lower, and repaid with gold any excess of imports it

might have. The gold going into the low-cost country then, had the effect of increasing the price level in the low-cost country so that the price levels of the two countries again became in balance. That theory has now gone by the board; and apparently the only law which governs the rate of exchange is the law of currency supply and demand.
Canadians buy so much more in the United States than Americans buy from us that there is an acute shortage of American dollars. Thus far the foreign exchange control board has supplied the deficiency, but it is now at the end of its tether. The effect of more Canadian dollars being offered in the United States market than are required to pay for Canadian goods purchased by Americans would ordinarily be to drive down the value of the Canadian dollar until we stopped our over-purchases.
Every economic proposition set out in. the textbooks is qualified by the statement, "other things being equal." But the difficulty in dealing with these questions as practical problems is that other things are seldom equal. Therefore it is always with the greatest difficulty that one can arrive at a safe conclusion as to what would .happen in any given set of circumstances.
The government's gazing into the crystal ball has thus far not been very successful; but we may be thankful there are economic laws which, after the government is through with its fumbling activities, after it has taken us from one mess into another, after having passed from one control to a stricter control, will enable us to revert to economic laws, so that we may pull ourselves out of the morass, oven if it is a most painful process.
May I pause here a moment to say that with the difficulties surrounding a broad economic question, such as a decision as to what our exchange rate should be, it seems to me that the members of the house would not be able to come to an intelligent decision without the use of the committees' system, where we may have before us those who make it their life's work to study these problems, so that we may draw upon the opinions of experts, for what they are worth, and so that we may have before us the businessmen and bankers who are experienced in these problems.
As it is, we have a parliamentary system which is probably England's greatest contribution to civilization. But one of the greatest features of that system is that it is a living organism and a living growth, and that it can grow according to the conditions it has to meet. We should come out of the nineteenth century and streamline our parliament. Without a committee in which these matters

Foreign Exchange Conservation
could be thoroughly gone into, powers must rest in the hands of the executive; and parliament-particularly the government majority-[DOT] can be nothing but a subservient majority. How can an individual member hope to go into intricate questions of a grave nature, such as what our exchange rate should be, and the restrictions we should put on, or what powers of life and death we should give to the ministry, unless we have capable advisers?
Certainly it is the system in the United States; and whether or not our parliamentary system allows for it, since its inception, times have changed so that if we are to do a job at all, and if we are to serve the people, then we must be given the opportunity of having before us people who will be able to give us the benefit of whatever information they may have, and so that we may interpret their views in the light of the needs of our constituents.
We have a whole host of other committees of the house; and I think it might be of interest to the people of Canada to know that, while apparently we cannot afford the time and personnel for a committee to go into this very grave problem-perhaps the greatest problem we shall have to face this session- yet we have a railway' committee with twenty-three members; another committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines composed of sixty members; a committee on printing with fifty-four members; a committee on the library of parliament with forty-four members; one on the restaurant with twenty-four members; one on Indian affairs with twenty-two members and one on canteen funds with twenty-two members. Compare the relative importance of those committees and the time devoted to them in this building with the importance of the problem now before the house.
The regulations the government has brought down in an endeavour at this late date to conserve our exchange and to restore the balance are not of a temporary nature, no matter what the minister may say. The condition of Canada's trade with the United States has shown a chronic lack of balance almost from the beginning of our economic history. An operation is required. The government's action is much like a medicine man telling you to hold a festered finger in the air instead of lancing it. These controls may well be fastened upon us, not for a matter of months or years, but forever. Certainly there is nothing in them which is of a permanent, corrective nature. They merely give a blood transfusion, as it were, and do nothing to cure the infection in the blood itself. Are we to
have restrictions forever in order to correct our exchange unbalance? Or are we to resort to more natural methods?
What can be considered to be the true value of the Canadian dollar in terms of United States currency? Three per cent Dominion of Canada bonds due in 1966 sell for around 104 in Canada, but those same bonds bring only 87 in New York, a difference of 17 points. If anyone wants to know the true value of the Canadian dollar, it is about 15 or 16 per cent discount. The foreign exchange control board have issued a little pamphlet in an endeavour to show that the free money market in Canadian funds in New York is only a small market which does not mean anything, that it is not for current merchandise transactions but only for investment account. The fact is that every week hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of Canadian bonds are traded in New York by life insurance institutions and others. They are willing sellers and willing buyers. The price of those bonds in New York is 87, whereas the price in Canada is 104. May I say that it was not always 87; it was 102i on July 16, 1946. Some time after our revaluation, our bonds began to go down in price because the United States investor foresaw exactly where the Liberal government would bring the Canadian economy. It has rendered us destitute of United States reserves and nothing has been done for many months to restore those reserves. We now have a reflection of what Canadian credit is in that country.
Let the Minister of Finance try to raise a loan in New York at the present time repayable in Canadian dollars. He will soon find that the true value of our exchange is about fifteen per cent discount. Canadians are regarded as being honest people and they are entitled to honest dollars vis-a-vis the United States. As it is now, we have several kinds of dollars just like Germany had under. Schacht; we have many kinds of currency.
When the Minister of Finance spoke the other day he said that there was nothing to suggest that currency depreciation would solve our problem. May I say that that is the good old-fashionied way to prevent over-buying of goods in another country. Would putting our dollar down to ninety cents help us to balance our currency vis-a-vis the United States? I suggest that a ten per cent depreciation of our dollar wouldi increase our exports to the United States.

I am just saying that you could increase your exports. I thought you said that you had not enough steel in Canada, and yet you say you are exporting it. The revaluation of the dollar would be an automatic process when we have no controls. When these things are left to the natural working of the economic laws they bring into being self-righting forces. Those forces would be brought into effect after artificial controls had been removed.
We have a great deal of surplus war capacity. The minister can give the house the actual figures because he knows all the answers to these questions. I suppose that there was an increase of fifty per cent in our industrial capacity during the war and some of that capacity is not being used at the present time. It could be used if there were a ten per cent devaluation in the United States market.
I am glad to see the minister is enjoying this so much because, as I say, he knows it all. If there is anything at all in the Geneva agreements under which tariffs are cut a certain amount; if we are to be helped by the Geneva agreements through such cuts, what would 'be the effect in Canada of an exchange devaluation? The effect of a ten per cent cut would be similar to a lowering of tariffs against us by ten per cent. Will the minister deny that? I shall willingly accede him the floor if he wishes to deny that a ten per cent devaluation will do just as much
as a ten per cent cut in the tariffs of foreign countries.

Does my hon. friend realize
that there is a United States component in practically everything we use and that that would cost us ten per cent more? A cut in tariff is a straight cut in the cost of the goods, but a depreciation in currency means that, while we would get more for what we sell, we would also have to pay more for what we buy. Therefore it is not equivalent in any way, shape or form.

Do I understand the minister to say that we would go back to this particular debate tomorrow?
